name: Every recorded screen the ledger lists can be read back — snapshots are addressable by id
notes: REWRITTEN (one snapshot per date) by developer. The journey itself is unchanged and still holds: every screen the ledger lists is individually addressable by id, and selecting one drives GET /research/desk/screen?id=<id> -- a plain read that recomputes nothing and writes nothing. What changed is the evidence it can be shown with. The previous version clicked the TWO same-date recordings of 2026-07-27 (936543601e75 / 3ad3c57aa6ba), which was the sharpest available proof precisely because the store's old 5-pin key let one date accumulate copies: any bar top-up -- including bars for days AFTER the screen date, which cannot change one of its rows -- re-keyed the date and wrote a second file. That is the defect this change removes (app/research/desk_screen_decision.py settles a date on every run; app/research/desk_screen_cleanup.py collapsed the six dates already carrying copies), so a same-date pair no longer exists to click. The script now clicks two DIFFERENT dates instead, asserting each snapshot's own id and created_utc in the Provenance panel -- the same addressability claim, over evidence the product still produces.

Every assertion here is SUPERSEDE-PROOF, deliberately. A date's snapshot is now replaced whenever its bars genuinely move, so its 12-hex id suffix and its created_utc both change over the rig's lifetime while the date's addressability -- the thing this journey is about -- does not. So the id assertions match on the stable prefix 'screen-2026-07-27-' / 'screen-2026-07-29-', and the previous version's created_utc pins ('2026-07-27T21:42:14.636275Z') are replaced by the viewing banner, which names the date rather than the recording. Pinning a suffix or a timestamp would make this script assert the store's current contents rather than the product's behaviour, and would go red on the next honest refresh of either date.

DROPPED: the previous step 4 asserted the coverage-divergence note's 'ranked row(s) in this screen show every timeframe badge dark'. Only screen-2026-07-27-936543601e75 satisfied it (3 of its 63 ranked rows -- NFLX/META/NVDA -- carried all four timeframe badges dark); the surviving 2026-07-27 recording (3ad3c57aa6ba, the newer of the pair) has zero such rows, and no other snapshot in the store has any. That evidence was deliberately superseded by the cleanup, not quietly lost -- the divergence note itself still ships and is unchanged.

This script is SAFE to replay repeatedly: selecting a calendar day only drives GET /research/desk/screen?id=<id>. It clicks `desk-history-day` cells (the year-at-a-glance calendar that replaced the Screen History table), each carrying both data-screen-date and data-screen-id; the calendar opens on the displayed snapshot's own year, so 2026's recorded days are visible without paging.
Step 7 is a post-match liveness check (this era's iter-4/iter-5 lesson): a further /desk navigation AFTER the key assertions match, proving the page is still alive and rendering correctly.
